blurb: Dr. K hosts: Loughran & McDonald (2011) gave computers a finance dictionary — and a counting rule. You become the counter: fifty words, two lists, one net tone. Watch out for the words that look negative and aren't.
intro: Dr. K here. Computers can't read — they count. So in 2011, Loughran and McDonald gave them a finance dictionary and a counting rule. This episode, you become the counter: fifty words, two lists, one net tone. Watch out for the words that look negative and aren't.

body: In 2011, Loughran and McDonald asked a simple question: what happens when you count sentiment in 10-Ks with a general-purpose word list? The answer was a warning. About 73.8% — nearly three-fourths — of the negative word counts produced by the Harvard-IV dictionary in 10-Ks are words that are not negative in finance at all: tax, cost, capital, liability, board, vice. A tax is a fact of business, not a complaint; a board is a group of directors, not a piece of lumber.
It gets worse: words like mine, cancer, and crude mark an industry, not an event — a mining company, a drug trial, an oil producer. A general dictionary reads the word and misses the world.

So Loughran and McDonald built finance-specific lists instead. Their paper — “When Is a Liability Not a Liability? Textual Analysis, Dictionaries, and 10-Ks”, Journal of Finance 66(1), 35–65 — gives the LM agent its evidence. The lists ADAM uses: Positive, Negative, Uncertainty, Litigious, Constraining, and Modal (strong and weak). Approximate, version-dependent sizes: Positive ~354, Negative ~2,337–2,355, Uncertainty ~297, Litigious ~904, Strong Modal 19, Weak Modal 27. Constraining (~184 words) is a later addition from Bodnaruk, Loughran & McDonald (2015) — it was not in the original 2011 six, but it belongs to the same family.
lessons.h: Why a general dictionary fails in finance
lessons.tip: Before trusting any sentiment score, ask which dictionary produced it. A score built on the wrong word list is confident, precise, and wrong.

body: LM's own measures are proportions. Count the list words, divide by the total words in the passage: % Positive = Positive ÷ total words, % Negative = Negative ÷ total words, and net LM tone = (Positive − Negative) ÷ total words. Per 1,000 words is the same measure rescaled: (count ÷ total words) × 1,000.

Here is the teaching passage — 50 words, written in 10-K style, invented for this lesson: “Strong demand helped sales improve this year, and efficient operations delivered a clear benefit to shareholders. Management expects continued success from new products. However, revenue faced a decline in one segment, a loss on discontinued operations, and higher risk from volatility, leaving the outlook weak and a burden on margins.”

Count it by hand. Positive (5): strong, improve, efficient, benefit, success. Negative (6): decline, loss, risk, volatility, weak, burden. No other word in the passage is on either list — “expects”, for example, is not an LM Positive word, and “operations” appears twice but is on neither list.
The arithmetic: %Pos = 5 ÷ 50 = 10.0%; %Neg = 6 ÷ 50 = 12.0%; net LM tone = (5 − 6) ÷ 50 = −0.02 (−2.0%). Per 1,000 words: Positive 100, Negative 120, net −20 per 1,000 words.

One formula you will NOT see here as LM's: (Positive − Negative) ÷ (Positive + Negative) = −1 ÷ 11 = −0.091. That is Henry's (2008) tone measure — widely used with LM lists, but not LM 2011's formula. Same sign, different magnitude: which is why the formula matters as much as the words.
lessons.h: How sentiment is calculated — the worked example
lessons.tip: Try the counter below before you trust the numbers above. Click every word you think is on a list — then reveal the answer and see which of your picks the dictionary disagrees with.

body: The LM agent's strength is that it is transparent and auditable: every point of its score can be traced to a specific word on a published list. If you disagree with the score, you can open the list and argue about the word. No black box, no mystery weights.

Its limit is that it is context-blind. It counts words, not sentences. Negation defeats it: “not expected to face a loss” still counts “loss” as negative. Legal language defeats it: litigious terms are not the same as distress. And it cannot tell fresh news from boilerplate — a risk paragraph repeated unchanged for five years scores exactly the same as one written yesterday.
That is why ADAM keeps LM as one agent among three — never as the whole verdict. Its evidence is real, but it is lexical evidence only, and the adjudicator needs to know what it cannot see.

game.done: Counted, checked, and honest about the limits. A dictionary is a good witness — and a bad judge.

game.intro: The 50-word passage, one more time — but now you do the counting. Build the score, slot by slot.
game.title: Dr. K Challenge: Score the passage

lessons.h: Strengths — and the limits that matter
lessons.tip: A dictionary can tell you a passage contains the word “risk” six times. It cannot tell you whether the risk is new, whether it matters, or whether the sentence actually says the opposite. That is the rest of the system.

outro: You counted like LM counts — and you saw the trap: a dictionary sees words, not sentences. “Not expected to…” will fool it every time. Next, a model that actually reads the sentence: FinBERT.

quiz.q: In the 50-word worked example, what are the LM % Positive and % Negative?
quiz.why: Positive 5 ÷ 50 = 10.0% and Negative 6 ÷ 50 = 12.0%. “100 and 120” are the per-1,000-words counts, and −0.02 is the net tone, not a percentage.

quiz.q: Which of these is LM 2011's own net tone formula?
quiz.why: LM 2011's measures are proportions of total words: net tone = (Positive − Negative) ÷ total words = −0.02 in the worked example. (Positive − Negative) ÷ (Positive + Negative) = −0.091 is Henry's (2008) tone measure — a different formula, not LM's.

That is why finance needs its own lists.
